titleEn: COPD Exacerbation - Salbutamol, Ipratropium and CPAP

patient.name: Margaret Doyle
patient.affectEn: alert but exhausted and frightened; sitting bolt upright on a kitchen chair, leaning forward on her elbows (tripod position), pursed-lip breathing, using her neck muscles to breathe; home nasal cannula on; refuses to lie down
patient.speechEn: speaks only one or two words at a time between breaths; her daughter fills in most of the history. Cooperative and follows instructions.

scene.settingEn: Small, overheated ground-floor apartment in Nanaimo at 0815 hrs; room about 26 degrees C. A home oxygen concentrator is running in the corner with its tubing across the floor. No lit smoking materials. The patient sits on a kitchen chair; her anxious daughter is beside her, talking over her. One patient.
hazardsEn: home oxygen concentrator running, tubing across the floor - a trip hazard and an oxygen-safety consideration (no lit smoking materials present)
infectious respiratory presentation (fever, productive cough) - mask as part of PPE

bystanders.knowsEn: She called 911 this morning. Her mother has COPD and home oxygen at 2 L/min. Three days of worsening breathlessness with a productive cough and green sputum, fever yesterday; much worse since 0600 this morning. She used her blue inhaler many times this morning without relief (she has lost count). Two hospital admissions for COPD in the past year. She is anxious and talks over her mother, but answers whatever she is asked and will hold doors or move furniture if asked.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
salbutamol nebules and salbutamol MDI with spacer
bag-valve mask with PEEP valve, oral and nasal airways
surgical masks / respirator masks for PPE
PCP only: epinephrine for IM injection

dispatchEn: 0815 hrs. Code 3 to a ground-floor apartment in Nanaimo. 71-year-old female with known COPD, increasing shortness of breath over three days, now unable to speak in full sentences. Her daughter called. Hospital is 10 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: she has home oxygen and has used her blue inhaler many times this morning without relief.
arrivalEn: The daughter opens the door of a small ground-floor apartment. It is overheated - about 26 degrees C. A home oxygen concentrator hums in the corner and its tubing runs across the floor to the patient. No lit smoking materials. The patient sits bolt upright on a kitchen chair; the daughter, anxious, starts talking over her mother as soon as you walk in. One patient.
firstLookEn: A 71-year-old woman sitting bolt upright on a kitchen chair, leaning forward on her elbows in a tripod position, pursed-lip breathing, neck muscles straining with each breath, her home nasal cannula in place. She looks up, too breathless to say more than a word or two.

primary.locEn: Alert (AVPU = A) and oriented, but exhausted. Speaks one or two words at a time. Will not lie down.
primary.airwayEn: Clear and self-maintained. No secretions, no stridor.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 32, laboured with marked accessory muscle use, prolonged expiration, audible wheeze, pursed-lip breathing. On auscultation: widespread expiratory wheeze with poor air entry at both bases.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 118, regular. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Modified rapid body survey for a medical patient: barrel chest, no trauma, no pedal edema, no calf swelling. Skin pale with dusky lips, warm and moist (skin is given automatically during the RBS). No trauma - c-spine not indicated.
primary.skinEn: pale with dusky lips, warm and moist

history.ccEn: Can't... breathe. (Daughter: "Her breathing has been getting worse for three days and now she can't finish a sentence.")

opqrst.oEn: Three days. (Daughter: "It came on gradually over three days, and it got much worse at about 0600 this morning.")
opqrst.pEn: Sitting up... helps. (Daughter: "Sitting forward like this helps a little; she can't lie down at all. Her blue inhaler helped at first, but not now.")
opqrst.rEn: No... pain. (Daughter: "No chest pain. It doesn't go anywhere.")
opqrst.sEn: Worst... since hospital. (Daughter: "This is the worst she's been since her last admission.")
opqrst.tEn: All the time. Worse. (Daughter: "Constant, and it keeps getting worse.")

history.painScoreEn: She shakes her head: "No... pain." (No chest pain; no numeric pain score is given in this scenario.)

sample.sEn: Breathless... coughing. (Daughter: "Three days of getting more short of breath, coughing up green phlegm, and she had a fever yesterday.")
sample.aEn: None. (Daughter: "No allergies that we know of.")
sample.mEn: Puffers... oxygen. (Daughter: "Her blue salbutamol inhaler - she's used it lots of times this morning, I've lost count, and it isn't helping. Tiotropium. Home oxygen at 2 litres. And amlodipine for her blood pressure.")
sample.pEn: COPD. (Daughter: "COPD - she's been admitted twice in the past year. She smoked for years - 50 pack-years - and quit 2 years ago. High blood pressure. No heart problems.")
sample.lEn: Tea. (Daughter: "Just tea this morning. She's had a poor appetite for two days.")
sample.eEn: Just... worse. (Daughter: "Nothing happened - she's been getting worse for three days with the cough and the green phlegm, and it got much worse at about 0600.")

fe.generalEn: Feverish... not eating. (Daughter: "She's been feverish and off her food for two days.")
fe.cnsEn: No. (Daughter: "She's not confused - that's her normal. No headache.")
fe.respiratoryEn: Green... phlegm. (Daughter: "Green sputum, no blood in it, no chest pain. She's much worse than her usual.")
fe.cardiovascularEn: No. (Daughter: "She always sleeps on two pillows - that's no different. No ankle swelling, no palpitations.")
fe.eentEn: Sore throat... last week. (Daughter: "She had a sore throat and a runny nose last week.")

findings.headNeckEn: Pursed-lip breathing, accessory neck muscle use. No JVD.
findings.chestLungsEn: Barrel-shaped chest, hyperresonant. Widespread expiratory wheeze at all 6 sites with poor air entry at both bases; no crackles. After bronchodilators (and CPAP for a PCP), air entry improves and the wheeze is reduced.
findings.backEn: Posterior auscultation confirms the same findings: widespread expiratory wheeze, poor air entry at both bases, no crackles. No sacral edema.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: No pedal edema. No calf tenderness.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Nicotine staining of the fingers, no clubbing change. Circulation, sensation and movement intact.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline before medication; SpO2 84% on her home 2 L nasal cannula, rising to 90% on high-flow oxygen; temperature indicated (infectious symptoms); BGL not indicated. CPAP eligibility (PCP): RR above 24, SpO2 under 94% on oxygen, accessory muscle use, awake and following commands, systolic above 90 - she qualifies
vitalsSets.skin: pale with dusky lips, warm moist
vitalsSets.spo2: 84% on 2 L NC, 90% on high flow

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: PCP course only: after salbutamol/ipratropium and about 10 minutes of CPAP, en route; improving - air entry improved, wheeze reduced. (No set-2 values are scripted for a course without CPAP; set 1 values persist.)

resp.depth: less laboured, accessory muscle use reduced
resp.character: less laboured, improved air entry with reduced wheeze

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: Her lips are still dusky and she is tiring; she can still only manage one or two words.
Her level of consciousness is falling: she is drowsy and can no longer follow your commands.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan nebulizer with salbutamol and ipratropium, oxygen, BVM with PEEP, CPAP (PCP), and a stretcher to the door
triggers: bring the stretcher to the door

expected.actionEn: Anticipate that this patient must not be walked - bring equipment and the stretcher to her
triggers: we'll bring the stretcher to her
bring everything in so she doesn't exert herself

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (oxygen tubing trip hazard, oxygen safety, overheated room), environment, nature of illness (respiratory distress), one patient
triggers: oxygen tubing is a trip hazard

expected.actionEn: Don gloves, eye protection, and verbalize a mask given an infectious respiratory presentation
triggers: surgical mask for the infectious symptoms

expected.actionEn: First look: tripod position, pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscle use, one-to-two-word sentences
Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert (but note exhaustion - a falling LOC would signal impending failure)
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Verbalize c-spine not indicated
Assess airway
triggers: she's talking so her airway is open

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing thoroughly: rate, depth, effort, accessory muscle use, air entry and wheeze
Auscultate the chest as part of the SOB assessment - the guideline lists auscultation explicitly
triggers: poor air entry at the bases

expected.actionEn: Assess circulation
Modified rapid body survey appropriate to the presentation (barrel chest, edema, calf swelling)
Note skin: pale with dusky lips, warm moist
Apply HIGH-FLOW oxygen: a COPD patient complaining of SOB with SpO2 84 percent requires high-flow oxygen titrated to a target of 94 percent - do not withhold oxygen for fear of hypoxic drive
triggers: high flow is indicated even with COPD

expected.actionEn: Keep her sitting upright and leaning forward; do not lay her flat and do not let her walk
Categorize as RTC and act with urgency
Transport after the first salbutamol dose, ready to load within 15 minutes
Delegate the partner to prep egress and bring the stretcher to the patient; manage the anxious daughter
triggers: daughter, can you get her medications

expected.actionEn: Establish chief complaint: worsening shortness of breath
HxC/C with OPQRRRST/LOTARP plus a respiratory-specific history: sputum, fever, orthopnea, puffer use and effect, comparison with previous exacerbations
triggers: how many times did you use your puffer
is this like your previous flare-ups

expected.actionEn: PMHx incl COPD severity, admissions and smoking history
Medications incl how many puffs she has already taken this morning
Allergies
LOI
GCS with components
BP by auscultation - required before CPAP (systolic must be above 90)
Pulse rate/strength/rhythm
Respirations rate/depth/character - the key vital in this call
Skin hands-on
Pupils
SpO2 with calibration; record the change with each oxygen and drug intervention
triggers: check the waveform matches the pulse

expected.actionEn: Temperature - indicated with infectious respiratory symptoms
FE - General health (fever, appetite)
FE - CNS (baseline mentation)
triggers: is this her normal mental status

expected.actionEn: FE - Respiratory (pertinent: sputum, hemoptysis, baseline exercise tolerance)
triggers: how is this compared to your usual

expected.actionEn: FE - Cardiovascular (differentiating COPD from CHF: orthopnea, edema)
triggers: how many pillows do you sleep on

expected.actionEn: FE - GI/GU
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (recent URTI)
Head/neck exam incl JVD and accessory muscle use
Chest exam with 6-site auscultation before and after bronchodilators, comparing bilaterally
triggers: auscultate before and after the neb

expected.actionEn: Abdomen exam
Back exam with posterior auscultation and sacral edema check
Lower extremities - edema and calf tenderness to screen for CHF and DVT
Upper extremities
Initiate the SOB protocol with correct sequence: position, oxygen, auscultate, baseline vitals, then salbutamol, then transport
triggers: position, oxygen, auscultate, vitals, then salbutamol

expected.actionEn: Salbutamol 5 mg by nebulizer (or MDI with spacer) with the 6 rights, repeated as required
triggers: right patient right drug right dose

expected.actionEn: PCP: ipratropium 500 mcg as a SINGLE dose combined in the same nebulizer as salbutamol
PCP: dexamethasone 8 mg PO
PCP: apply CPAP only after confirming ALL indications and NO contraindications; start at 5 cmH2O with 5 L/min and titrate in 2.5 cmH2O steps to a maximum of 10
Verbalize the deterioration plan: remove CPAP and ventilate with BVM plus PEEP if she can no longer maintain respiratory effort
triggers: if she deteriorates I'll remove CPAP and bag her
BVM with PEEP if she tires
if her LOC drops we take off the CPAP
if she tires I'll assist ventilations with the BVM

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs and all interventions after each drug, each CPAP change and each move
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes with a repeat auscultation to document the response
Titrate oxygen and CPAP to the SpO2 target and document each change
If LOC falls: remove CPAP and ventilate with a BVM plus PEEP valve at 5 cmH2O
triggers: remove the CPAP and start bagging
ventilate with the BVM and PEEP at 5
if her LOC falls I'll remove CPAP and ventilate with PEEP
if she can't keep breathing on her own I'll assist with the BVM

expected.actionEn: En-route notification for a critical respiratory patient
Complete hand-off with drugs, CPAP settings, SpO2 trend and auscultation findings
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate lets the patient stand up or walk (to the stretcher, the door or the ambulance) - any self-exertion
candidate lays the patient flat / supine (instead of keeping her sitting upright and leaning forward)
candidate keeps her on her home nasal cannula at 2 L/min or other low-flow oxygen and does not give high-flow oxygen, e.g. because of COPD / hypoxic drive concerns

PCP verbalizes checking CPAP indications and contraindications before applying it (awake and following commands, systolic above 90, no vomiting / aspiration risk, no pneumothorax, no trauma, no tracheostomy, mask fits)
PCP applies CPAP incorrectly: starts above 5 cmH2O, increases by more than 2.5 cmH2O per step, goes above the 10 cmH2O maximum, or leaves a poor mask seal uncorrected
after being told her LOC has fallen and she can no longer follow commands, candidate keeps CPAP on instead of removing it and ventilating with a BVM (plus PEEP)
PCP sets the PEEP valve above 5 cmH2O to start, increases by more than 2.5 cmH2O per step, goes above 10 cmH2O, or keeps PEEP on when systolic falls below 90 or she arrests

drugs.doseEn: 5 mg by nebulizer, or 4 x 100 mcg by MDI with a spacer (adult; MDI and spacer strongly recommended with infectious respiratory symptoms); repeat as required; transport after the first dose; after baseline vitals
drugs.cautionsEn: coronary disease; COPD patients with degenerative heart disease; diabetes

drugs.doseEn: 500 mcg by nebulizer, combined with salbutamol in the same nebulizer - SINGLE dose only (salbutamol may be repeated); MDI alternative 160 mcg (8 x 20 mcg)
drugs.cautionsEn: not for monotherapy - acts with salbutamol; narrow-angle glaucoma; prostatic hyperplasia or bladder neck obstruction

drugs.contraindicationsEn: systemic fungal infection; hypersensitivity to dexamethasone or other corticosteroids
drugs.cautionsEn: heart failure or hypertension (fluid retention) - she has hypertension

drugs.doseEn: start at 5 L/min with the CPAP valve at 5 cmH2O; obtain a facial seal; reassess patient and vitals; increase in 2.5 cmH2O increments to a maximum of 10 cmH2O (oxygen flow per the CPAP setting table: 5 cmH2O = 5 L/min, 7.5 = 7, 10 = 8). If she deteriorates: remove CPAP and ventilate with a BVM (consider PEEP).
drugs.indicationsEn: 13 years or older in significant respiratory distress, awake and following commands, maintains a patent airway, and RR > 24, SpO2 < 94% on oxygen and accessory muscle use - she qualifies
drugs.contraindicationsEn: 12 years or less; decreased LOC or inability to follow commands; respiratory arrest or hypoventilation / imminent respiratory failure; unable to fit the mask; vomiting or other aspiration risk; traumatic cause; tracheostomy; suspected or known pneumothorax; systolic BP < 90 mmHg

drugs.doseEn: PCP only: 0.5 mg IM every 5-20 minutes for severe bronchospasm with impending arrest; consider when SpO2 < 90% and/or moderate to severe bronchospasm is unresolved with salbutamol
drugs.cautionsEn: further hypotension if administered too quickly

notificationFacts.cc: COPD exacerbation - severe shortness of breath, unable to speak more than one or two words
notificationFacts.hxcc: three days of worsening shortness of breath with productive green sputum and fever, much worse since 0600; own inhaler ineffective this morning; two admissions in the past year
notificationFacts.vitals: on arrival RR 32 laboured with accessory muscle use, SpO2 84% on her home 2 L (90% on high flow), BP 158/88, pulse 118, temperature 38.1; now RR 24, SpO2 93% on CPAP 7.5, BP 142/84, pulse 106
notificationFacts.treatments: kept upright and carried, high-flow oxygen, salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 500 mcg by nebulizer at 0824, dexamethasone 8 mg PO, CPAP 5 titrated to 7.5 cmH2O (PCP); ETA 10 minutes
notificationFacts.findings: widespread expiratory wheeze with poor basal air entry, no crackles, no JVD, no peripheral edema - infective exacerbation rather than pulmonary edema

handoffFacts.cc: worsening shortness of breath in known COPD, now unable to speak more than one or two words
handoffFacts.hxcc: gradual onset over three days with productive green sputum and fever, much worse since 0600; blue inhaler used many times this morning without relief; worst since her last admission; no chest pain, no orthopnea beyond her usual two pillows, no leg swelling
handoffFacts.initialVitals: GCS 15, BP 158/88, pulse 118 regular, RR 32 laboured with accessory muscle use, skin pale with dusky lips warm moist, pupils equal and reactive, SpO2 84% on 2 L nasal cannula rising to 90% on high flow, temperature 38.1 tympanic
handoffFacts.finalVitals: GCS 15, BP 142/84, pulse 106 regular, RR 24 less laboured, skin pink warm moist, pupils equal and reactive, SpO2 93% on CPAP 7.5 cmH2O, temperature 38.1; improved air entry with reduced wheeze

handoffFacts.treatments: kept upright leaning forward and carried out; high-flow oxygen titrated toward 94%; salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 500 mcg combined by nebulizer at 0824 (ipratropium single dose); dexamethasone 8 mg PO; CPAP started at 5 and titrated to 7.5 cmH2O; BVM with PEEP on standby

Salbutamol 5 mg neb, repeated as required

examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: She is breathing fast and hard: marked accessory muscle use, prolonged expiration through pursed lips, audible wheeze.

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR gives salbutamol 5 mg by nebulizer or 4 x 100 mcg by MDI with a spacer, repeated as required, plus positioning (upright, not walked), high-flow oxygen titrated toward 94 percent, auscultation and rapid transport. EMR does NOT have ipratropium, dexamethasone, CPAP or IM epinephrine for bronchospasm. If she deteriorates, EMR assists ventilations with a BVM. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds ipratropium 500 mcg as a single combined nebulizer dose, dexamethasone 8 mg PO, CPAP from 5 cmH2O titrated in 2.5 cmH2O steps to a maximum of 10 cmH2O with matched oxygen flow (after confirming every indication and no contraindication), a PEEP valve on the BVM if ventilation becomes necessary, and epinephrine 0.5 mg IM for severe bronchospasm with impending arrest. Functional Enquiry en route, kept brief.

sourcePages: Scenario md-05 (data/practical/scenarios.json): dispatch, scene, primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions, ongoing (LOC falls if CPAP is misapplied), handoff. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (respiratory distress / accessory muscle use = unstable); p.49 SOB With History of Asthma/COPD (seated leaning forward, limit movement; oxygen to maintain SpO2 >= 94% - caution: may not be achievable; auscultation; transport immediately or delegate egress; history and baseline vitals; salbutamol by nebulizer or MDI, transport after the first dose; MDI and spacer with influenza-like illness; PCP: ipratropium combined with salbutamol, single dose; IM epinephrine for SpO2 < 90% and/or bronchospasm unresolved with salbutamol; consider dexamethasone; consider CPAP); p.50 Oxygen Administration (high-flow oxygen for COPD patients complaining of SOB is indicated; nasal cannula 1-3 L/min only following acute care; titrate to a maximum of 15 L/min, NRB 15 L/min, consider CPAP (PCP), PEEP for PCPs); p.51-53 CPAP (PCP) and CPAP Guidelines (indications, contraindications incl. decreased LOC and systolic < 90; start 5 L/min at 5 cmH2O, 2.5 cmH2O increments to a maximum of 10 cmH2O; if she deteriorates remove CPAP and use BVM; PEEP 5 cmH2O, 2.5 increments to a maximum of 10, remove if systolic < 90 or arrest; CPAP setting table); p.62 Dexamethasone (8 mg, PO preferred; caution hypertension); p.66 Epinephrine (0.5 mg IM every 5-20 minutes for severe bronchospasm with impending arrest, PCP); p.70 Ipratropium (500 mcg nebulized, single dose; not monotherapy); p.77 Salbutamol (5 mg nebulized, MDI 4 x 100 mcg adult, repeat as required).
